photo.title: A standing group portrait of a hunter and two Mandari women, one with a breast-feeding baby and a young girl standing in front. The woman to the right is smoking a pipe and wearing a metal disk fringed goat-skin apron with two bead waist strings, as well as a cloth breast covering and bead neck ornaments. She also shows a number of scarification marks on her abdomen and arm, it being unclear whether these were intended to be decorative. The young girl is wearing a single waist string of beads and a neck ornament, a common set of ornaments for young children. The man has a goat-hair tassel attached to his arm and a goat-hair decorated quiver, bow and spear (for hunting), as well as some sort of hand weapon or ornament. He is wearing European-style shorts and no display bead strings, possibly suggesting that he is married. The women's skin skirts also suggest that they may be married, and that this may be a family group.

Two women, one seemingly breast-feeding a toddler, sit underneath a shelter or granary on a mat, with some crops, probably ground-nuts, on the floor nearby. The woman in the foreground has her hair shaved at the sides to leave a central section. In the section of cultivation seen beyond are stalks of ripening millet. Since groundnuts and some millet were harvested in August and September, this suggests that these women are taking a break from harvesting activity probably during the hottest part of the day.

A woman, girl and smaller children sit underneath a shelter or granary on a mat, with some crops, probably ground-nuts, on the floor nearby. In the section of cultivation seen beyond are stalks of ripening millet. Since groundnuts and some millet were harvested in August and September, this suggests that these women are taking a break from harvesting activity probably during the hottest part of the day.

A three-quarter length portrait of a woman wearing a waist cloth and holding a pipe in her mouth, standing amongst tall maize plants. Around her neck are a variety of bead and metal chain ornaments. In another image she is described simply as an unmarried girl.

A three-quarter length portrait of a girl wearing a waist cloth and holding a small child on her hip, standing amongst tall maize plants. Around her neck are a variety of bead and metal chain ornaments. She is also wearing a lip and earrings.

A three-quarter length portrait of a woman wearing a waist cloth and holding a pipe in her mouth, standing amongst tall maize plants. Around her neck are a variety of bead and metal chain ornaments. In another image she is described simply as an unmarried girl.

A three-quarter length portrait of a girl wearing a waist cloth and holding a small child on her hip, standing amongst tall maize plants. Around her neck are a variety of bead and metal chain ornaments. She is also wearing a lip and earrings.

Two Mandari women wearing checked waist cloths, neck ornaments and leg rings, standing on dead wood logs with a section of maize field in the background. Maize ripened and was harvested in July and August.

A group of Mandari children. A girl is wearing a waist string with a fringe of ?leather pieces hanging down from metal links and is holding a gourd on her head. In front of her is a small boy with distended stomach carrying a baby on his back in a sling. An older boy, also with a distended stomach, sits on a rock above them watching. It is likely that these children are quite malnourished judging from their stomach distension.
A group of several Mandari children sitting in the grass near a settlement, one girl with her arm resting on the back of a sheep.

A group of Mandari women and children resting in the shade of a tree. They are displaying a variety of styles of hair shaving, and a couple are wearing the display beads commonly given by youths to girls that they admire.

A three-quarter length portrait of two Mandari youths dancing, with arms gesturing in imitation of the training of the horn of their favourite ox [partial double exposure at top]. The training of ox horns for aesthetically pleasing effects is carried out by most Nilotic cattle-keeping groups. One arm is curved forwards in imitation of the training of the left horn across the muzzle. The other arm curves upwards and to one side. The youth to the right is also wearing the waist string beads of a particular age set.

A youth places his hand on the shoulder of a girl standing in a raised position beside him, a pipe in her mouth and temples shaved. She is wearing a number of beads, probably given to her by male admirers such as this youth.

A three-quarter length group portrait of a youth and a girl wearing a checked waist-cloth, with other youths standing in a line beside them. She is wearing a number of beads around her neck, probably given to her by male admirers such as the youth standing beside her. She and the youths to her left have also prominent forehead scarification after the manner of the Dinka, although for the Mandari it does not denote any formal initiation (hence her use of it along with the youths), and was used instead for aesthetically pleasing effect.
A group portrait of a number of Mandari girls sitting under a tree, one in the foreground in a deck chair.

An upper body portrait of two Mandari girls wearing waist-cloths and strings of beads around their necks, one leaning against the thatch of a hut. Beads worn by girls around the neck were often given by male admirers. They both have forehead scarification after the manner of the Dinka, and the girl in the foreground has a series of linear scar marks on her abdomen, although for the Mandari it does not denote any formal initiation (hence her use of it along with the youths), and was used instead for aesthetically pleasing effect.

A head-and-shoulders group portrait of a Mandari youth resting his hands on the shoulders of a girl either side of him. The girls are wearing strings of neck beads, probably gifted to them by their male admirers, and the girl in the foreground has forehead scar patterns in the manner of the Dinka, although for the Mandari this did not constitute part of an initiation process.

A full-length group portrait of three Mandari girls wearing checked textile waist-cloths, strings of neck beads (often gifted by male admirers) and single plumes in their hair. Beyond to the right can be seen a youth wearing a set of waist beads denoting an age set, and carrying a club.

A full-length group portrait of three Mandari girls wearing numerous strings of beads around their waists, a youth standing to their left with another youth's arm around him. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women.

An upper body portrait of a Mandari girl wearing strings of beads around neck. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women. She also has scarification patterns on her forehead after the manner of the nearby Dinka, as well as decorative lines on her abdomen. These did not indicate any initiation procedure however but were done for aesthetically pleasing effect only.

A three-quarter length group portrait of four Mandari girls wearing strings of beads around their necks and waist cloths. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women. They also have scarification patterns on their foreheads after the manner of the nearby Dinka. These did not indicate any initiation procedure however but were done for aesthetically pleasing effect only.

A full length group portrait of some young Mandari girls standing in the shade of a thicket, carrying gourd water containers in net carriers. They have decorated their hair and faces using an ash mixture.

A full length frontal portrait of two Mandari girls with ash decorated faces, wearing checked waist cloths and several strings of neck beads, one a coin pendant. Harvested beans are laid out on the ground in the sun behind them to dry.

A three-quarter length portrait of two Mandari girls wearing textile waist cloths and strings of beads around their necks [blurred image], other children gathered near them at the edge of the frame. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women.
A portrait of two Mandari women (probably married women) sitting in the shade of a large tree, wearing textile body cloths and a string of large beads around their necks.
A full length group image of five young Mandari women wearing textile body cloths, standing in a homestead. One of them is smoking a pipe.
A three-quarter length portrait of two Mandari women standing in the shade of a large tree with their arms around each other, wearing textile body cloths and strings of beads around their necks.

A full length portrait of a Mandari man wearing a thick and expensive ivory arm ornament, with three boys (probably sons) in their homestead, standing next to two wooden shrine stakes (ködi lo jok). The family would sometimes make offerings to such shrines to spiritual powers, for instance after diagnosis by a Mandari doctor regarding illness caused by a malevolent spirit. The shrine stake thereby stands for the presence of a spirit within the family dwelling.

A full length portrait of a Mandari woman with two girls, one carrying a baby and a gourd water container in a carrying net. The other girl is carrying a large basketry covered container on her head. They are all wearing colourful beads in a variety of colours around their necks and waists. Such bead strings were often given to young women by courting male youths.

A three-quarter length portrait of two young Mandari women in a cattle camp wearing yellow textile body cloths and a large number of mostly red bead strings around their waist, as well as some around the neck [partial double exposure]. Such bead strings were often given to young women by courting male youths. Youths wear such rem beads as a way of denoting their age grade grouping and for display.

A three-quarter length portrait of two young Mandari women in a cattle camp wearing textile waist cloths and a large number of mostly red bead strings around their waist, as well as some around the neck [poor negative]. Such bead strings were often given to young women by courting male youths. Youths wear such rem beads as a way of denoting their age grade grouping and for display.
A three-quarter length portrait of a Mandari man wearing several strings of waist beads standing with two young women in a homestead, the step thatch of a hut visible behind them [poor photo].
An upper body full face portrait of two Mandari youths in a homestead wearing strings of waist beads, a club tucked under one arm.
A three-quarter length portrait of two Mandari women wearing textile body cloths, strings of beads, and metal arm ornaments.

A full length portrait of a Mandari woman wearing a checked textile body cloth, with a baby tied to her back. She is also carrying a gourd vessel in a string carrier and on her head a roll of matting. Across the foreground Jean Buxton's shadow wearing a skirt is visible, looking down into her Rolleiflex camera.
A head-and-shoulders portrait of a Mandari youth wearing a textile head-wrap.
An upper body full face portrait of a Mandari youth wearing a textile head-wrap and plume, with string of flat-face beads around the base.
An upper body full face portrait of a Mandari youth, with ash-treated hair.

An upper body full face portrait of a Mandari youth, wearing a number of strings of rem waist beads. The colour configuration of these beads exhibited relative age-grade status. Age-grades among the western Mandari seem to have been a relatively recent, loosely defined or organized borrowing by youths from their Atuot neighbours, there being no memory of age-grades or even initiation in the past.

An upper body full face portrait of a Mandari youth, wearing a number of strings of rem waist beads. The colour configuration of these beads exhibited relative age-grade status. Age-grades among the western Mandari seem to have been a relatively recent, loosely defined or organized borrowing by youths from their Atuot neighbours, there being no memory of age-grades or even initiation in the past.

A full length portrait of a Mandari woman wearing a leather apron leaning against a fence with a pipe in her mouth [poor photo]. Just visible behind her, propped against the fence, is a bicycle presumably belonging to Jean Buxton.
Two Mandari women sitting on a low square platform in a homestead, with a girl sitting next to them. The women are wearing bound metal arm and leg ornaments.

A three-quarter length portrait of a Mandari woman leaning against the thatch of a hut, wearing metal arm ornaments and a short fringed apron. She has several bands of vertical cicatrice dots on her abdomen.

A three-quarter length portrait of a Mandari woman leaning against the thatch of a hut, wearing metal arm ornaments and a short fringed apron. She has several bands of vertical cicatrice dots on her abdomen.

A three-quarter length portrait of a man wearing a tunic, holding a small parrying shield and spear (possibly abat, large type used for hunting Buffalo etc.). In the background is a section of garden with manioc growing.

A young woman with a black ostrich plume in her hair standing on the steps of a raised lomore or courting hut in western Mandari. There were one or more such huts in a homestead belonging to a lineage or extended family, and were places where girls of courting age met young men in the evenings and slept there overnight. A white band painted around the entrance makes them known to others as a lomore.
A group of five men sitting together in the shade of a tree, smoking long pipes with clay bowls and stems with sections of metal.

A group of young Mandari men seated on the ground, several of whom are holding spears. On their heads some are wearing textile head wraps. Just beyond them a woman with a small child are also sitting on the ground.
A group of young Mandari men seated on the ground, several of whom are holding spears. On their heads some are wearing textile head wraps.

A full length group portrait of two men in uniforms of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) wearing a belted tunic and a hat with regimental plume, two women in floral European-style dresses standing beside them. Both men have their heads turned half away from the camera, perhaps a military style. Beyond them is a long stone and brick built rectilinear building with a dodgy thatched roof, perhaps a barracks?

A full length group portrait of five men in uniforms of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) wearing a belted tunic and a hat with regimental plume. Beyond them is a long stone and brick built rectilinear building with a large thatched roof, perhaps a barracks?

A full length group portrait of a man in the uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) holding a rifle and wearing an ammunition belt and hat with plume. Beside him stand three women wearing beaded ornaments and metal armrings. Another man wearing European clothes as well as a large ivory arm ornament, is partially visible to left of frame.

A formal portrait of a seated man in a military uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955), possibly ranking as a sargeant, with five women and two children posing around him, all wearing Mandari ornaments and clothing. Behind them is a large rectilinear thatched building, probably a communal building for soldiers and their dependants. These women may be wives or family members of the soldier living with him at the military post.

A group portrait of three standing men, one in the uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) wearing a belted tunic and a hat with regimental plume. The other two men wear administration-style shirt and shorts, and may have been employed by the administration locally. Behind them another man stands next to Buxton's vehicle, parked outside a hut.
A three-quarter length portrait of a man in the uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) holding a rifle over his shoulder and wearing an ammunition belt and hat with plume.
A full length portrait of a man in the uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) presenting a rifle outside a hut, wearing an ammunition belt and hat with plume.

A portrait of Jean Buxton with camera, sitting on the verandah of a brick building of the colonial administration, probably in Tali. Next to her is the Mandari sergeant, Makelele Nyayo, who was charged with looking after her personal safety.

A portrait of Jean Buxton's Mandari sergeant, Makelele Nyayo, who was charged with looking after her personal safety, sitting cross-legged on the verandah of a colonial brick building next to a girl wearing beaded neck ornaments. Just behind or to the side of the girl another person gestures a hand into the frame above her head.
A close-up portrait of Jean Buxton's Mandari sergeant, Makelele Nyayo, who was charged with looking after her personal safety, sitting on the stoep of a colonial brick building.

arms.title: Spear with ebony point set into a incomplete wooden shaft, with the junction covered by a double hide sheath [RTS 12/7/2005].
Spear with horn point set into an incomplete wooden shaft, with a hide sheath covering the junction and decorated with a brass ring [RTS 26/7/2005].
